blogData.short_description: Ronin, Wormhole, Nomad, Poly Network, BNB Bridge, Multichain: six ways bridges lose locked assets, and what your product must build to avoid it.
blogData.content:
Cross-chain bridges have incurred losses of about $2.9 billion through 34 attacks between 2021 and Q3 2025 (Global Ledger). Bridge attacks have been responsible for about $2 billion in losses in 2022 alone, which was 69% of the total amount of cryptocurrency stolen in that year (Chainalysis). The problem for founders developing exchange, wallet, or DeFi products where assets cross blockchain networks is not whether bridges can be attacked, but whether the product can survive it.

Cross-chain products open real opportunities for founders, who also carry the duty of keeping their users' assets safe in the bridges they rely on. A bridge failure may result in significant financial losses and damage to customer relationships.

Past blockchain bridge attacks have exposed security weaknesses in validator permissions, message validation, and smart contracts. The task is to build a product that stays safe when any one of those components fails. 

How Cross-Chain Bridges Put Locked Assets at Risk

A cross-chain bridge refers to a service that enables users to transfer their assets across various blockchain networks. This typically includes locking the asset in one blockchain network and creating an equivalent on another blockchain network.

This may include scenarios such as when a user deposits ETH in a bridge contract on the Ethereum blockchain. Once the deposit is validated, the bridge will create an equivalent token on the destination blockchain.

This includes various stages such as:

  • Validating the deposit on the source blockchain.
  • Validator or messaging layer permissions.
  • Cross-chain messaging.
  • Release or minting of assets on the destination blockchain.
  • Asset accounting and withdrawals.

All these stages may present various security threats since:

  • If the destination contract accepts any fake message, attackers may create tokens without validating the deposit.
  • Validator credentials being hacked, leading to unauthorized approval of transactions. These are the core bridge vulnerabilities, because one blockchain cannot verify another's transactions on its own.
  • For founders, the main priority is clear: never release assets based only on an external message claiming that a deposit has been made.

Six Major Cross-Chain Bridge Failure Patterns

The following incidents demonstrate six different weaknesses that product teams should consider during architecture planning.

Validator Key Compromise – Ronin Bridge

The attack on the Ronin Bridge highlighted how poor validation security could make significant digital assets vulnerable to theft. In case a significant proportion of control lies with just a few validators, hackers can take advantage of the stolen keys to make unauthorized transactions.

As per the post-mortem by Ronin Network, hackers exploited five out of the nine validator keys (four owned by Sky Mavis and one by Axie DAO). These keys helped the hackers to withdraw 173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC (around $625 million).

What users experienced:  

Users faced deposit and withdrawal disruptions after the attack. The unauthorized withdrawal of funds on March 23, 2022, went unnoticed for six days. The breach was discovered on March 29, when a user's attempted 5,000 ETH withdrawal failed because the bridge no longer had sufficient funds to process it.
 

What founders must build:

  • Distribute validator keys: Distribute validator keys across independent operators rather than having the keys held by one entity.
  • Secure the private keys: Secure the private keys using hardware security and limiting access.
  • Establish withdrawal caps: Limit the amount of transactions that can be performed and implement emergency pause features to limit any losses.
  • Track validator activity: Track the activities of validators and any suspicious transactions.
  • Establish real-time alerts: Activate real-time alerts for large or unusual withdrawal transactions within minutes, not days.

The Ronin hack highlights a vital security lesson: multiple validators are not a guarantee of security when most of the signing authority is controlled by one entity.

Signature Verification Failure – Wormhole

The Wormhole Hack shows why all accounts and transactions should be verified by the bridge during the signature verification process. If the bridge does not verify the account properly, attackers will be able to bypass the security measures, sign the approvals, and steal funds from them.

According to Elliptic, the vulnerability was found in the Solana-side smart contract of the bridge. During the signature verification process, the smart contract allowed a spoofed system account, so a forged guardian approval passed verification and the attacker minted 120,000 wrapped ETH without depositing any ETH. No ETH was used for that minting. The value of stolen assets was approximately $325 million.

What users experienced: 

Wormhole decided to suspend its activity until they managed to solve the problem of security. Users worried whether the original ETH still backed their wrapped assets. In the end, the company named Jump Crypto, Wormhole's parent company, replaced the 120,000 ETH within a day. 

What founders must build:

  • Cross-chain message processing: Validate all accounts involved in cross-chain message processing before confirming a transaction.
  • Valid guardian signatures: Ensure signatures originate from appropriate and authenticated public keys.
  • Invalid messages: Do not allow messages containing any erroneous information or involving an unauthorized account.
  • Testing: Test the verification process for all steps, including communication with other external systems, to identify security flaws.

The example of Wormhole reveals that checking signatures is not sufficient; the bridge needs to validate accounts and messages.

Incorrect Message Validation – Nomad

As per the Mandiant Report by Google Cloud, the Nomad Bridge exploitation came about when the smart contract update created a trusted message root value of 0x00, which the bridge also considered a valid root value. The coding error enabled the attackers to create messages with zero root values and call the process() function without going through the verification process. As such, the unverified messages were accepted, and attackers were able to make withdrawals. Not long after that, many other people used the technique to withdraw around $190 million worth of crypto from the bridge's liquidity pool.

What users experienced:  

The funds of the bridge were withdrawn too fast, and the process of withdrawal became unpredictable for users.

What founders must build:

  • Confirm initial parameters: Make sure all significant parameter values have been tested before using or upgrading smart contracts.
  • Refuse default parameters: Refuse zeros or nulls as valid data for verifying any transaction.
  • Test negative cases: Try to figure out how your bridge will behave when receiving an incorrect message root.
  • Ask for a security audit: It is necessary to ask independent security experts to audit the upgrades and other crucial changes in your smart contracts.
  • Implement emergency controls: Make sure your bridge can safely stop message processing when unusual activity is detected.

As we saw in the Nomad case, even small issues in the initial configuration can result in significant financial losses. Founders should always test all critical settings and security checks before deploying cross-chain bridges.

Privileged Access and Authorization Failure – Poly Network

This Poly Network hack proved how vulnerable inadequate administration and cross-chain permissions could make the platform.

The attacker took advantage of weaknesses in communication between key contracts, such as the cross-chain manager and the contract determining the keepers' permissions. The attacker managed to alter permission settings using privileged actions and transfer assets on multiple blockchain platforms.

More than $600 million worth of digital assets was involved at the beginning. Yet, most of the stolen assets were eventually returned.

What users experienced: 

Cross-chain transfers were disrupted, and Tether froze approximately $33 million in stolen USDT. Nearly all the stolen assets, worth over $600 million, were all returned by 25 August 2021, about two weeks later, once Tether released the frozen USDT , restoring access to affected funds. 

What founders must build:

  • Role-based access control for restricting administrative actions.
  • Separation of permissions for verifying messages from permissions for managing assets.
  • A requirement for several permissions to perform configuration changes.
  • Tracking of all privileged transactions.

Permissions should be considered a high-risk financial control, not an application setting.

Merkle Proof Verification Failure – BNB Bridge

The BNB Bridge attack proved why the founders should take care to ensure that the cryptographic proofs are verified accurately.

The attackers were able to take advantage of a loophole present in the IAVL proof-verification mechanism that was being used by BSC Token Hub. They forged a proof that the bridge accepted as valid.

They were able to mint approximately two million BNB tokens, which were worth roughly $586 million at the time of the attack. (according to Coinbase's investigation  – BSC Token Hub Compromise Investigation and Analysis) This forced the validators to shut down the chain temporarily to conduct an investigation into the matter.

What users experienced: 

Operations on BNB Chain were disrupted temporarily as the validators carried out their investigation into the attack.

What founders must build:

  • Use proven and reviewed cryptography-based proof-verification schemes.
  • Check for Merkle proof invalidation, incompleteness, and tampering.
  • Verify the blocks and transaction proofs of the source chain.
  • Use stringent validation steps before issuance on the destination chain.

Cryptographic validation is an essential security mechanism. The fact that the proof has been validated does not necessarily mean it is valid. The validation scheme needs to be secure too.

Centralized Key Management Failure – Multichain

The Multichain hack has illustrated how over-reliance on some key individuals might lead to serious security breaches in a decentralized blockchain project.

In July 2023, an attack led to the withdrawal of about $125–130 million from several Multichain bridges without any authorization. (CoinDesk reported: CoinDesk – Multichain Bridges Experience Unannounced Outflows of Over $130M)  The funds were held in the project's infrastructure operated by the MPC technology. Subsequently, the Multichain team revealed that it had lost access to its MPC keys after the CEO was detained by Chinese police. This left the project unable to manage its bridge operations normally and highlighted the risks of relying heavily on a small number of individuals for critical key management.

What users experienced: 

Users were advised to stop using the service and revoke their contract approvals. Bridge transactions got stuck, and the team could not provide a clear timeline for when services would resume.

What founders must build:

  • Ensure that key signing processes are not reliant on a single individual.
  • Distribute key management and administrative tasks among various individuals who can be trusted.
  • Develop and implement a recovery plan in case any key personnel become unavailable.
  • Be on the lookout for any odd withdrawals or any other changes within the key management system.

Six Security Controls Founders Should Build Into Their Bridges

Real-life incidents act as a real-world basis for establishing security standards for products. Entrepreneurs should learn from such experiences and implement testable control measures.

How to Design a Secure Cross-Chain Bridge Architecture

A secure cross-chain bridge must be built on the concept of independent verification.

The source chain needs to verify that the transaction did indeed occur. Cross-chain messaging security ensures that every transaction message is authenticated before the destination contract approves the transfer. The destination contract needs to independently verify that the message is authorized, unprocessed, and relates to the correct asset in the specified amount.

Also, the design of the bridge needs to incorporate:

  • Replay prevention – avoid authorizing further transfer for a message that has already been processed.
  • Rate limiting – restrict abnormally high-volume or rapid withdrawals.
  • Pausability – pause relevant bridge processes in case of detected anomalous behavior.
  • Asset accounting – reconcile locked assets, issued tokens, and released funds.
  • Upgradability – require independent verification of critical contract changes.

One important thing to consider is finality. A product must not release any destination assets based on transaction inclusion in source chain blocks but must take into consideration source chain confirmation and finality properties.

Lastly, the bridge must have a well-defined recovery process in case of failure to process the message, transaction, or delay in its transmission.

Why Continuous Monitoring and Incident Response Matter

Security does not stop after a bridge contract passes an audit. Blockchain technology keeps changing, and new security risks can appear due to integrations, network updates, system dependencies, or human mistakes.

Founders should set up monitoring systems to check:

  • Unusual withdrawals and repeated failed transactions.
  • Suspicious validator activities and signing behavior.
  • Differences between locked assets and tokens available on the destination chain.
  • Unexpected smart contract updates or changes in admin permissions.

The team should also have a clear plan for handling security issues. It should define who can pause transactions, who investigates the problem, how users are informed, and how lost assets are handled.

Regular security checks and emergency practice sessions are also important. These help the team understand how to respond quickly when a major system or security issue occurs.

Monitoring and recovery must be part of the original architecture, not features added after an incident. 

How Justtry Builds Cross-Chain Products

Development of the blockchain bridge is not limited to linking several chains. It entails the creation of an architecture that would secure the transfer of assets, verify cross-chain messaging, and enable businesses to deal with unexpected circumstances.

The following components make up our strategy at Justtry Technologies:

  • Integration of Bridge and Messaging Layers: The choice of proper bridge protocols and cross-chain messaging layers depending on the architecture of the product.
  • Destination-Chain Independent Validation: Cross-chain message and transaction validation on the destination chain before asset transfers.
  • Transaction and Daily Transfer Limits: Implementation of per-transaction and daily transfer limits to reduce risks related to unusual withdrawal behavior.
  • Emergency Pause Mechanisms: Development of pause mechanisms that would stop bridge operations in case of suspicious behavior.
  • Monitoring and Security Audits: Transactions monitoring and security audits performed independently by a third party before the mainnet launch.

Want to build a multi-chain exchange or wallet? Contact us today!

Conclusion

The Ronin, Wormhole, Nomad, Poly Network, BNB Bridge, and Multichain incidents show why bridge security is important. Founders must focus on secure development, proper verification, access control, and regular security checks. Founders who understand these risks before launch protect their users' assets and their own reputation. Ultimately, a secure cross-chain platform starts with security built into its architecture, not added as an afterthought.

faqs.question: What are the most common cross-chain bridge security vulnerabilities?
faqs.answer: Common cross-chain bridge vulnerabilities include compromised validator keys, signature verification failures, incorrect message validation, privileged-access issues, Merkle proof verification flaws, and centralized key management. These weaknesses can allow attackers to bypass security checks and move assets without authorization.

Bridge attacks can result in stolen collateral, unbacked wrapped tokens, delayed withdrawals, suspended deposits, and inaccessible funds. Users may also lose confidence in the platform if the development team cannot provide a clear recovery plan.
faqs.question: How do cross-chain bridge hacks affect users' locked assets?
Can smart contract audits prevent cross-chain bridge hacks?
faqs.answer: Smart contract audits help identify vulnerabilities in transaction validation, access control, and contract logic before deployment. However, audits cannot guarantee complete security. Continuous monitoring, secure infrastructure, upgrade testing, and incident response planning are also necessary.

faqs.question: How do we choose a bridge for a multi-chain exchange?
faqs.answer: Choose a bridge based on its security audits, validator model, supported networks, transaction fees, speed, and recovery options. Make sure it fits your exchange's security and scalability requirements before integration.
